::: {.why}
A long-only constraint improves out-of-sample performance for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone's view on shorting, and knowing the reason tells you when it will stop helping.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Explain why a no-short constraint is equivalent to shrinking the covariance matrix in a specific direction.
- Report the out-of-sample effect of three constraint regimes on your own data and say which you would use.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the section of the Boyd and Vandenberghe convex optimization book on duality as far as complementary slackness, then look at the dual variables your CVXPY solution returns for the binding constraints. The shadow price on a position cap tells you how much the objective wanted to violate it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Demonstrate the equivalence numerically: solve the unconstrained problem with a covariance matrix shrunk toward the identity at several intensities, and find the shrinkage level whose weights most closely match the long-only solution. The correspondence will not be exact and the direction is the point.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the practical conclusion in your notebook: constraints help when the estimation error is large relative to the true dispersion of means, which is a statement you can check rather than a preference.
:::
:::
